Designing a Cart Management System (Amazon / Flipkart / JioMart)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites:Caching and Message Queues

TL;DR

A cart management system lets users add, remove, and update items before checkout. The hard parts: persisting carts across devices, handling flash sales (1M users adding the same item), merging guest carts on login, and keeping prices/stock accurate without slowing down the add-to-cart path.

In 3 sentences: User adds items to cart → stored in Redis for sub-ms reads and async-backed to DynamoDB for durability. On cart view, the service enriches items with live price and stock status from downstream services. At checkout, inventory is reserved with a distributed lock to prevent overselling.💡 A distributed lock is a claim recorded in one shared store so that, across dozens of application servers, only one checkout at a time may act on a given item. Without it “is it in stock” and “take it” are two steps that other buyers can slip between.

1. Understanding the Problem

A shopping cart is the bridge between browsing and buying. Every e-commerce platform needs one, and despite looking simple (just a list of items), it has to handle: millions of concurrent carts during sales, real-time stock awareness, device switching (add on phone, checkout on laptop), guest-to-login transitions, flash sales where 100K users add the same item simultaneously, and graceful degradation when downstream services (inventory, pricing) are slow or down.

Think Amazon Cart, Flipkart Cart, Myntra Bag, or Zepto Cart.

2. Naive First Cut

User adds item → write a row to Postgres → read it back on cart page. Works for 100 users.

How it breaks at scale:

  • Flash sale: 500K add-to-cart/sec → Postgres row-level locks choke at ~50K writes/sec
  • Cart page load queries Postgres every time → 10M concurrent users = 10M reads/sec on one DB
  • Guest carts with no user_id are awkward to model in a relational schema
  • No separation between hot (active session) and cold (abandoned 3 weeks ago) carts
  • Price and stock checks embedded in the write path → add-to-cart latency spikes when inventory service is slow
  • Single region DB → users across India see 50-200ms latency depending on geography

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Amazon Cart Service — Uses a session-based in-memory store backed by a durable persistence layer. Carts are eventually consistent; inventory is checked at checkout, not at add-time.💡 Eventually consistent means a change may take a moment to be visible everywhere, and that is accepted deliberately. A cart that shows a five-second-old price is fine; a stock count that lies at the moment of payment is not, which is why the strictness is concentrated at checkout. Learn more → Guest carts merge on login using a deterministic merge strategy. (Amazon Builder’s Library patterns)
  • Flipkart Cart Architecture — Redis-first with MySQL backup. Cart operations are sub-10ms. During Big Billion Days, the cart service handles 1M+ ops/sec by sharding Redis across 100+ nodes. (Flipkart Engineering)
  • Shopify Cart — Stores cart as a JSON document in a KV store. Cart is schema-flexible (different stores have different item attributes). Uses optimistic concurrency with version numbers to handle race conditions.
  • Walmart Labs — Uses a write-behind cache pattern: write to cache immediately, async-persist to DB. If cache fails, fallback to DB reads. Cart merge uses “last-write-wins” per item with timestamps.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Add, remove, update items — user adds an item to cart, changes quantity, or removes it. Response in <100ms.
  2. Persistent cross-device cart — logged-in user’s cart survives app close, device switch, and browser restart. Guest carts persist via session cookie (7-day TTL).💡 TTL = time to live, the age at which the store deletes the record by itself. Guest carts getting a 7-day TTL is how abandoned anonymous carts clean themselves up without a scheduled job.
  3. Real-time cart enrichment — when user views cart, each item shows current price, stock status (in stock / only 2 left / out of stock), and delivery estimate.

Below the Line

  • Cart merge (guest → logged-in) on login
  • Apply coupon / promo codes
  • Save for later (wishlist-like behavior)
  • Cart sharing (share a link with pre-filled cart)
  • Cart-level validations (max items, max quantity per item, seller restrictions)
  • Cart expiry policies (remove items after 30 days)
  • Flash sale quantity limits (“max 1 per customer”)

5. Non-Functional Requirements

  • Cart size limits for denial-of-service (DoS) prevention (max 500 items)

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Users: 50M DAU (daily active users), 10M concurrent carts during peak
  • Write QPS: 500K add/update/remove per second at peak (flash sale)💡 QPS = queries per second. Half a million writes a second is the number that rules out an ordinary relational database on the add-to-cart path, and it is driven entirely by the flash sale rather than by normal trade. Learn more →
  • Read QPS: 2M cart-view reads/sec at peak (users refreshing cart page)
  • Storage: Average cart = 5 items × 200 bytes = 1KB. 50M active carts × 1KB = 50GB (fits comfortably in Redis cluster)
  • Bandwidth: ~16 Gbps at peak for cart API responses (2M reads/sec x ~1KB), which is why the cart page is served from the hot store and never rebuilt per request

7. Core Entities

  • Cart — id, userId (or guestSessionId), items[], version, updatedAt, expiresAt
  • CartItem — itemId, sellerId, quantity, priceAtAdd, addedAt
  • InventoryReservation — reservationId, cartId, itemId, quantity, status (HELD/CONFIRMED/RELEASED), expiresAt
  • CartEvent — eventType (ITEM_ADDED/REMOVED/QUANTITY_CHANGED/CART_MERGED), userId, itemId, timestamp, metadata

8. API / System Interface

POST /v1/cart/items
  Body: { itemId, sellerId, quantity }
  Response: { cartId, items[], totalItems, version }
  Auth: JWT (logged-in) or Session cookie (guest)
  Note: Idempotent via clientRequestId header. Does NOT check inventory (fire-and-forget add).

PATCH /v1/cart/items/{itemId}
  Body: { quantity }
  Response: { cartId, items[], version }
  Note: quantity=0 is equivalent to DELETE

DELETE /v1/cart/items/{itemId}
  Response: { cartId, items[], version }

GET /v1/cart
  Response: { cartId, items[{ itemId, quantity, currentPrice, stockStatus, deliveryEstimate }], totalAmount, version }
  Note: Enriched response — each item has LIVE price and stock from downstream services.
  Auth: JWT or Session cookie

POST /v1/cart/merge
  Body: { guestSessionId }
  Response: { cartId, items[], mergeConflicts[] }
  Note: Called on login. Merges guest cart into user cart.

POST /v1/cart/checkout
  Response: { orderId, reservationId, paymentUrl }
  Note: This is where inventory gets RESERVED (locked). Not before.

Security notes:

  • userId comes from the JSON Web Token (JWT), never from request body (prevent cart tampering)💡 A JWT is a signed token the client sends with every request; because the server signed it, the user id inside can be trusted. Reading the user id from the request body instead would let anyone edit anyone’s cart. Learn more →
  • Rate limit add-to-cart: 50 requests/min per user (prevents bot abuse during flash sales)
  • Guest carts are tied to session cookie; no cross-session access

9. High-Level Design

FR1: Add / Remove / Update Items

The most frequent operation, and the one users judge the product by. A cart has to survive the user closing the app, so it has to be durable, and it has to be right — nobody should be able to add something that is not for sale.

Build the direct version: one service, one durable store, and a check against inventory so we never put an unavailable item in a cart.

New components:

  1. API Gateway — rate limiting, auth, routing
  2. Cart Service — core business logic for cart operations
  3. DynamoDB — the cart itself. Partition key userId, one item per sort key, so a cart is a single-partition read and an add is a single-item write.💡 The partition key decides which machine a record lives on; the sort key orders records within that partition. Choosing userId as the partition key means one person’s whole cart sits on one machine, so reading it is a single trip instead of a query across the cluster. Learn more →
  4. Inventory Service — answers “is this item available right now”, consulted before we accept an add.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User taps “Add to Cart” for SKU_123, quantity 1
  2. API Gateway validates the JWT and extracts userId. The user is taken from the token, never the body — otherwise anyone can write into anyone’s cart
  3. Cart Service asks the Inventory Service whether SKU_123 is available
  4. If it is, write the item to DynamoDB: userId as partition key, SKU_123 as sort key, with quantity, seller, the price at the time of adding, and a timestamp
  5. Return 200 OK

Why store priceAtAdd rather than just the item id? Because the price can move between adding and checking out, and the user needs to be told. Keeping the price they saw is what makes “this went up from ₹999” possible later; recomputing it would silently erase the change.

What we have deliberately left broken. Carts are durable, cross-device by construction, and never contain unavailable items. Three things do not survive the traffic this system is built for:

  • Step 4 writes to DynamoDB on the critical path of every operation. At 500K cart ops/sec that is 43.2B writes a day; on-demand pricing at $1.25 per million write units is on the order of $54,000 a day for cart writes alone, and it adds 5-10ms to an interaction users expect to feel instant. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • Step 3 calls the Inventory Service on every single add. For one hot item in a flash sale, that is every one of those 500K requests asking about the same SKU. That is Deep Dive 1, and it is where the reasoning gets genuinely counterintuitive.
  • Nothing emits an event. The cart is a row that changes and nobody downstream can observe it, so there is no way to notice that 70% of carts are abandoned, let alone react. That is Deep Dive 4.

FR2: Persistent Cross-Device Cart + Guest Merge

User adds items on phone → closes app → opens laptop → cart is there. Guest browses without login → adds 3 items → logs in → those items appear in their saved cart.

New components:

  1. Session Service — maps a guest session cookie to a temporary cart id, so an anonymous browser gets a cart partition of its own
  2. Cart Merge Logic — handles conflicts when guest cart and user cart have overlapping items

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Guest browses → session cookie assigned → cart stored under partition key guest:{sessionId} with a 7-day TTL, so abandoned guest carts expire on their own
  2. Guest adds items → same flow as FR1 but keyed by sessionId instead of userId
  3. Guest logs in → frontend calls POST /v1/cart/merge { guestSessionId }
  4. Cart Service reads both partitions: the guest cart and the user’s existing cart
  5. Merge strategy: the guest cart is what the user was just looking at, so it wins. Write the guest items over the user’s cart
  6. Delete the guest cart
  7. Return the merged cart to the frontend

Cross-device persistence:

  • A logged-in user’s cart lives under their userId in DynamoDB
  • Any device authenticating with the same identity reads the same partition
  • No sync protocol needed, because there is only one copy and it is server-side

What we have deliberately left broken. Guest carts survive login and a cart follows the user between devices. The merge rule is where this quietly destroys work:

“Guest wins” means an item the user had saved on their account and not in the current guest session is silently deleted by logging in. Someone who added a MacBook last week on their laptop, then browses as a guest on their phone and signs in, loses the MacBook — and nothing told them. The reverse rule is no better: user-wins discards everything they just added as a guest, which is the more visible annoyance but the same bug.

The real problem is that the rule treats merging as a choice between two carts, when the user’s intent is almost always the union of them. That is Deep Dive 3.

FR3: Real-Time Cart Enrichment (Price + Stock)

When user opens the cart page, they don’t just see “iPhone × 1.” They see: current price (might have changed since they added it), stock status (“only 2 left”), delivery estimate, and a warning if price increased.

New components:

  1. Inventory Service — returns current stock level per item
  2. Pricing Service — returns current price (may differ from price-at-add-time)
  3. Catalog Service — returns item details (name, image, seller info)

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User opens cart page → GET /v1/cart
  2. Cart Service reads the raw cart — one query on the userId partition → returns {SKU_123: qty 1, SKU_456: qty 2}
  3. Cart Service calls downstream services IN PARALLEL (not sequential):
    • Inventory: POST /inventory/batch-check { itemIds: [SKU_123, SKU_456] } → {SKU_123: 15 in stock, SKU_456: 0}
    • Pricing: POST /pricing/batch { itemIds: [...] } → {SKU_123: ₹499 (same), SKU_456: ₹1299 (was ₹999)}
    • Catalog: POST /catalog/batch { itemIds: [...] } → {names, images, seller info}
  4. Cart Service assembles enriched response: 
    {
  "items": [
    { "itemId": "SKU_123", "qty": 1, "currentPrice": 499, "priceAtAdd": 499, "stock": "IN_STOCK", "stockQty": 15 },
    { "itemId": "SKU_456", "qty": 2, "currentPrice": 1299, "priceAtAdd": 999, "stock": "OUT_OF_STOCK", "priceChanged": true }
  ]
}
JSON
  5. Frontend shows: “Price increased ₹999 → ₹1299” badge and “Out of Stock — Remove” option

Graceful degradation: If the inventory service is slow or down → return the cart without stock info and show “checking availability…” on the frontend. The cart must NEVER fail to load because a downstream enrichment service is down. This is the one piece of resilience that belongs in the base design rather than a deep dive, because without it we have coupled the availability of the cart to the availability of three other services.

What we have deliberately left broken. The cart page shows live prices and stock, and degrades rather than failing. Two gaps, both at the moment of purchase:

  • Stock shown here is advisory and nothing holds it. Step 3 reports that 15 units exist; it does not set any of them aside. Between the user reading “15 in stock” and completing payment two minutes later, all 15 can be sold to other people, so the cart page confidently promises availability the system never reserved. That is Deep Dive 5.
  • A price change is reported but not honoured either way. We show “₹999 → ₹1299” and have no notion of holding the old price, nor of what happens if it changes again during checkout.

And the enrichment fan-out has its own cost: three batch calls per cart view, on a page users open constantly, against services that are busiest during exactly the sales when carts are opened most.💡 Fan-out = one incoming request becoming several outgoing ones. Here one cart view becomes three service calls, so our traffic multiplies by three on the way down and the slowest of the three sets the page’s latency. Learn more →

Pricing service Current price per item itemId → price, discounts Read-heavy, cacheable Redis cache + Postgres source Pricing microservice

Why Redis + DynamoDB (not just Postgres):

Cart is session-like data — high write rate, high read rate, no complex joins, flexible schema (items vary per seller). Postgres row locks collapse at 500K writes/sec. Redis gives sub-ms latency for the hot path. DynamoDB provides infinite-scale durability without managing shards.

11. Data Modeling

Redis (Hot Cart Store — active session carts):

Key: "cart:{userId}" → Hash
  Field: "items" → JSON [{ itemId, sellerId, quantity, priceAtAdd, addedAt }, ...]
  Field: "version" → Integer (optimistic concurrency)
  Field: "updatedAt" → Timestamp
TTL: 30 days (inactive carts expire)

DynamoDB (Durable Cart Store — backup and persistence):

Table: carts
  PK: user_id (String)
  Attributes: items (List of Maps), version, updated_at, expires_at
  GSI: session_carts — PK: session_id (for guest cart lookup)

Postgres (Inventory — stock levels with row locks at checkout):

CREATE TABLE inventory (
    item_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    seller_id UUID NOT NULL,
    quantity_available INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity_available >= 0),
    reserved_quantity INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE inventory_reservations (
    reservation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    cart_id UUID NOT NULL,
    item_id UUID NOT NULL,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,  -- HELD, CONFIRMED, RELEASED
    expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_reservations_expiry ON inventory_reservations(expires_at) WHERE status = 'HELD';
SQL

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Add item to cart Redis HSET cart:{userId} with updated items JSON + INCR version
Read cart (enriched) Redis + Pricing/Inventory Read Redis cart → parallel calls to pricing and inventory services
Guest-to-user merge Redis + DynamoDB Read guest cart by sessionId, merge into user cart, delete guest
Reserve inventory at checkout Postgres UPDATE inventory SET reserved_quantity = reserved_quantity + ? WHERE item_id = ? AND quantity_available - reserved_quantity >= ? (row lock)
Write-behind to DynamoDB Async Kafka event on cart change → DynamoDB writer persists
scroll →

How Cart-Inventory Interaction Works at Checkout:

  1. User clicks “Buy Now” → Cart Service reads current cart from Redis
  2. For each item: SELECT quantity_available - reserved_quantity AS available FROM inventory WHERE item_id = ? FOR UPDATE (row-level lock)💡 FOR UPDATE tells the database to hold that row for the rest of this transaction, so a second checkout for the same item waits rather than reading a number that is about to change. Learn more →
  3. If available >= requested: INSERT INTO inventory_reservations with status=HELD and expires_at = now()+10min
  4. UPDATE inventory SET reserved_quantity += requested WHERE item_id = ?
  5. All in one Postgres transaction — if ANY item is unavailable, entire txn rolls back (no partial reservations)
  6. A background sweeper releases expired reservations every minute: UPDATE ... SET status='RELEASED' WHERE expires_at < now() AND status='HELD'

12. Deep Dives

1) 500K people add the same iPhone in ten seconds. Should the cart even ask inventory?

Problem: Big Billion Days. iPhone listed at ₹39,999. 500K users click “Add to Cart” in the first 10 seconds. Only 1000 units available.

Bad: check inventory on every add-to-cart, which is exactly what FR1 step 3 does. It is the obviously correct thing and it is wrong here. The Inventory Service gets 500K reads/sec for a single SKU → hot key → collapses. Users see “item unavailable” errors.💡 A hot key is a single record that an outsized share of traffic all wants at once. The rest of the fleet can be idle while the one machine holding that record falls over, and more machines do not help until the key itself is split or the traffic is removed. Learn more →

check inventory on every add-to-cart, which is exactly what FR1 step 3 does. It is the obviously correct thing and it is wrong here. The Inventory Service gets 500K reads/sec for a single SKU → → collapses. Users see “item unavailable” errors.

Don’t check inventory at add-time. Let everyone add to cart freely. Check stock only on cart page view and at checkout. Show “limited stock” badge. First 1000 to checkout win.

Same as Good, but add a soft limit at the cart level. After the first 2000 add-to-carts for a flash-sale item, start showing “selling fast — checkout now” urgency messaging. Use Redis on a counter to track how many carts contain this item. This doesn’t block anyone but creates urgency and reduces phantom demand.

At checkout: use DynamoDB conditional write (or Postgres ) to atomically decrement inventory. If inventory hits 0, reject checkout for subsequent users. Their cart still has the item, but they see “sold out” when they try to pay.

Adding to cart is NOT a commitment to buy. Don’t waste inventory-service capacity on something that has a 70% abandonment rate.

2) $54,000 a day to write carts nobody will buy from. What is the cheaper trade?

Problem: We write to Redis first (fast) and async-persist to DynamoDB (durable). What if Redis crashes after the write but before the DynamoDB persist? User’s last few cart changes are lost.

Bad: write to DynamoDB synchronously on every cart operation, which is FR1 step 4. Put both numbers on it: 500K ops/sec is 43.2B writes a day, and on-demand at $1.25 per million write units that is about $54,000 a day — roughly $20M a year to store shopping carts, 70% of which are abandoned. It also adds 5-10ms latency to every add/remove (on-demand pricing).

write to DynamoDB synchronously on every cart operation, which is FR1 step 4. Put both numbers on it: 500K ops/sec is , and on-demand at $1.25 per million write units that is about — roughly $20M a year to store shopping carts, 70% of which are abandoned. It also adds 5-10ms latency to every add/remove (on-demand pricing).

Write-behind with Kafka as buffer. Cart Service writes to Redis AND publishes to Kafka. A consumer drains Kafka into DynamoDB in batches. If Redis crashes, Kafka still has the events → replay into DynamoDB → hydrate back to Redis from DynamoDB.

Same as Good + version vector on the cart. Each cart has a monotonically increasing field. Redis cart has version 47. DynamoDB has version 45 (slightly behind). On Redis failure:

3) Logging in deletes the MacBook they saved last week. What should a merge actually do?

Problem: Guest has: {iPhone: qty 2, AirPods: qty 1}. Logged-in cart has: {iPhone: qty 1, MacBook: qty 1}. User logs in. What does the merged cart look like?

Bad: the guest-wins overwrite FR2 built — write the guest cart over the user’s, losing the MacBook. The mirror rule is no better: user-wins loses the AirPods they just added. Either way the system destroys items the user deliberately chose, silently, as a side effect of signing in. Nothing errors and nothing is recoverable, because the overwritten cart is gone rather than merged.

the guest-wins overwrite FR2 built — write the guest cart over the user’s, losing the MacBook. The mirror rule is no better: user-wins loses the AirPods they just added. Either way the system destroys items the user deliberately chose, silently, as a side effect of signing in. Nothing errors and nothing is recoverable, because the overwritten cart is gone rather than merged.

Union of both carts. For conflicts (same item in both), take max quantity. Result: {iPhone: 2, AirPods: 1, MacBook: 1}.

Same as Good but with user transparency. Show a toast: “We added 1 item from your browsing session” or a merge summary. For quantity conflicts, default to max but let user adjust on the cart page. Log merge events to Kafka for analytics (how many users hit merge conflicts? is it causing confusion?).

Edge case: guest cart has item that’s now out of stock. Still merge it in — show “out of stock” badge. Don’t silently drop items.

4) 70% of carts are abandoned and nothing in the design can even notice. How do we react?

Problem: 70% of carts are abandoned. Can we nudge users back?

Bad: FR1 emits no events at all, so the only way to find an abandoned cart is to go looking for one — poll the database every hour for “carts not checked out in 24h.” At 50M carts that is a full scan of the table every hour to find a small changed subset, which is expensive, wasteful, and gets slower as the business grows. It is also coarse: the signal arrives up to an hour late, when the moment that actually converts is minutes after someone walks away.

FR1 emits no events at all, so the only way to find an abandoned cart is to go looking for one — poll the database every hour for “carts not checked out in 24h.” At that is a full scan of the table every hour to find a small changed subset, which is expensive, wasteful, and gets slower as the business grows. It is also coarse: the signal arrives up to an hour late, when the moment that actually converts is minutes after someone walks away.

Event-driven. Kafka consumer tracks events. If no event arrives within 24 hours for that userId, emit an event. Notification service sends push/email: “You left items in your cart.”

Tiered nudges:

Implementation: Use a delayed Kafka consumer (or Redis sorted set with fire-time) to schedule nudge events at each tier. Cancel all pending nudges if user checks out.

5) The cart said 15 in stock and held none of them. When do we actually reserve?

Problem: User has 2 iPhones in cart. They click “Proceed to Checkout.” Between clicking and completing payment (2-5 minutes), another user could buy the last iPhone. How do we prevent overselling?

Bad: FR3 reported stock without holding any of it, so the obvious fix is to reserve at the other end — decrement inventory on add-to-cart. That trades a promise we cannot keep for a worse problem: 500K carts hold 500K reservations and 70% of them are abandoned, so real customers can’t buy because inventory is “held” by abandoned carts.

FR3 reported stock without holding any of it, so the obvious fix is to reserve at the other end — decrement inventory on add-to-cart. That trades a promise we cannot keep for a worse problem: 500K carts hold 500K reservations and , so real customers can’t buy because inventory is “held” by abandoned carts.

Reserve inventory only at checkout initiation (when user clicks “Pay”). Use a TTL-based hold (10 minutes). If payment isn’t completed, hold releases automatically.

Conditional write with :



If condition fails (not enough stock), return “only X left, reduce quantity.” The conditional write is atomic — no two users can over-decrement.


TTL-based hold: write a reservation record . A sweeper restores inventory for expired reservations. Same pattern as BookMyShow seat locks.

How it works end-to-end:

  2. Cart event published to Kafka → consumed by DynamoDB writer (durability) and analytics pipeline
    3. 
 
  3. User views cart → Cart Service reads from Redis + enriches in parallel from Inventory, Pricing, and Catalog services
    4. 
 
  4. User logs in → Merge Handler combines guest cart with user cart, writes merged result to Redis
    5. 
 
  5. User proceeds to checkout → Inventory Service reserves stock with conditional write (DynamoDB or Postgres row lock)
    6. 
 
  6. If user abandons → Kafka-based timer fires nudge notifications at 2h, 24h, 72h intervals
    7. 
 
  7. If Redis fails → Cart Service falls back to DynamoDB reads (slightly slower but no data loss)
    8.

What’s Expected at Each Level


Mid-level


Design a basic cart with add/remove/get operations using Redis. Recognize the need for persistence beyond Redis. Propose DynamoDB or Postgres as backup. Understand why inventory shouldn’t be checked at add-time.


Senior


Propose the write-behind pattern (Redis + Kafka + DynamoDB). Discuss cart merge strategies. Explain flash sale handling without blocking the add-to-cart path. Design the enrichment layer with parallel calls and graceful degradation. Discuss the checkout reservation with conditional writes.


Staff+


Discuss multi-region cart consistency, version vectors for conflict resolution, cart-level rate limiting for bot prevention during flash sales, and the abandoned-cart recovery pipeline with tiered nudges. Quantify costs (Redis cluster sizing, DynamoDB on-demand pricing). Propose observability: which metrics distinguish a healthy cart system from a degraded one.




🎯 Key Takeaways


    
 
  • Redis for speed, DynamoDB for durability — write-behind pattern gives you both
    • 
 
  • Don’t check inventory at add-time — it adds latency and wastes capacity. Check at view-time (soft) and reserve at checkout (hard).
    • 
 
  • Cart merge on login — union of items, max(quantity) for conflicts, transparent to user
    • 
 
  • Flash sale: let everyone add, gate at checkout — 70% will abandon anyway
    • 
 
  • Enrich in parallel, degrade gracefully — if pricing service is down, show stale price with a “checking…” badge, don’t fail the cart load
    • 





Related Designs


    
 
  • BookMyShow (Ticket Booking) — same reservation-with-TTL pattern at checkout
    • 
 
  • Digital Wallet (PhonePe) — payment orchestration after cart
    • 
 
  • Rate Limiter — protecting cart API during flash sales
    • 





Related Concepts


    
 
  • Caching → — Redis as hot-path cache for cart data
    • 
 
  • Message Queues → — Kafka for write-behind, events, and abandoned-cart triggers
    • 
 
  • Database Replication → — Redis Cluster replication for HA
